newsitem.title: USA: Breast cancer survival rates improving.
newsitem.headline: Breast cancer survival rates improving.

text.p: Amid the controversy over what age women should begin to get mammograms, researchers say breast cancer rates are no longer surging and fewer women are dying from the disease.

"Since 1990, age-adjusted mortality rates have begun to fall," National Cancer Institute director Dr. Richard Klausner said on Thursday, as the institute announced recommendations that women in their 40s should get regular mammograms.
Here are some key facts about breast cancer:
-- More than 180,000 U.S. women will be diagnosed with breast cancer this year, and there will be more than 40,000 deaths.
-- The American Cancer Society says the relative chance of surviving five years after diagnosis is now 84 percent.

-- The odds fall drastically to one-in-five for someone whose cancer has already metastasized or spread to distant parts of the body, vs. 97 percent for a local lesion detected very early before there the cancer has spread.
--Overall, a woman's lifetime risk of developing breast cancer is one in eight. But that statistic is often misunderstood, since the risk is highest among older women.

-- According to the National Cancer Institute, for 100,000 women ages 40-49, there will be 163 breast cancer diagnoses and 29 deaths. That is the leading cause of death in this age group, but it is still relatively rare, translating into a 0.3 chance of death from breast cancer before age 50.
-- In contrast, for women in their 60s there are about 374 cases diagnosed in 100,000 women, and 91 deaths.
-- Breast cancer is not the leading killer of older women, or even the leading cancer killer. Lung cancer, usually tied to smoking, takes a bigger toll.
